each.etymology: OE. eche, ælc, elk, ilk, AS. ælc; a always + gelic like; akin to OD. ieg, OHG. , MHG. iegelich. Aye, Like, and cf. Either, Every, Ilk.

eager.etymology: OE. egre sharp, sour, eager, OF. agre, aigre, F. aigre, fr. L. acer sharp, sour, spirited, zealous; akin to Gr. a point; fr. a root signifying to be sharp. Cf. Acrid, Edge.

eagle.etymology: OE. egle, F. aigle, fr. L. aquila; prob. named from its color, fr. aquilus dark-colored, brown; cf. Lith. aklas blind. Cf. Aquiline.

eagre.etymology: AS. eágor, , in comp., water, sea, eágor-streám water stream, sea.

ear.etymology: AS. eáre; akin to OFries. áre, ár, OS. , D. oor, OHG. , G. ohr, Icel. eyra, Sw. öra, Dan. öre, Goth. auso, L. auris, Lith. ausis, Russ. ukho, Gr. audire to hear, Gr. av to favor , protect. Cf. Auricle, Orillon.

earl.etymology: OE. eorl, erl, AS. eorl man, noble; akin to OS. erl boy, man, Icel. jarl nobleman, count, and possibly to Gr. arshan man. Cf. Jarl.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

early.etymology: From Middle English erly , erlich , earlich , from Old English ǣrlīċ ( “ early ” , adjective ) , equivalent to ere +‎ -ly .

earn.etymology: AS. earnian; akin to OHG. arn to reap, aran harvest, G. ernte, Goth. asans harvest, asneis hireling, AS. esne; cf. Icel. önn working season, work.

earnest.etymology: AS. eornost, eornest; akin to OHG. ernust, G. ernst; cf. Icel. orrosta battle, perh. akin to Gr. oriri to rise.

earth.etymology: AS. eor; akin to OS. ertha, OFries. irthe, D. aarde, OHG. erda, G. erde, Icel. jör, Sw. & Dan. jord, Goth. airpa, OHG. ero, Gr. ear to plow.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

earwig.etymology: AS. eárwicga; eáre ear + wicga beetle, worm: cf. Prov. E. erri-wiggle.

ease.etymology: OE. ese, eise, F. aise; akin to Pr. ais, aise, OIt. asio, It. agio; of uncertain origin; cf. L. ansa handle, occasion, opportunity. Cf. Agio, Disease.

easel.etymology: D. ezel ass, donkey, hence, easel, or G. esel; akin to E. ass. See Ass.

east.etymology: OE. est, east, AS. eást; akin to D. oost, oosten, OHG. , G. ost, osten, Icel. austr, Sw. ost, Dan. öst, östen, Lith. auszra dawn, L. aurora (for ausosa), Gr. ushas; cf. Skr. ush to burn, L. urere. Aurora, Easter, Sterling.

easter.etymology: AS. eáster, eástran, paschal feast, Easter; akin to G. ostern; fr. AS. Eástre, a goddess of light or spring, in honor of whom a festival was celebrated in April; whence this month was called in AS. Eásterm. From the root of E. east. See East.

easy.etymology: OF. aisié, F. aisé, prop. p. p. of OF. aisier. See Ease, v. t.

eat.etymology: OE. eten, AS. etan; akin to OS. etan, OFries. eta, D. eten, OHG. ezzan, G. essen, Icel. eta, Sw. äta, Dan. æde, Goth. itan, Ir. & Gael. ith, W. ysu, L. edere, Gr. ad. Etch, Fret to rub, Edible.

eaves.etymology: OE. evese, pl. eveses, AS. efese eaves, brim, brink; akin to OHG. obisa, opasa, porch, hall, MHG. obse eaves, Icel. ups, Goth. ubizwa porch; cf. Icel. upsar-dropi, OSw. opsä-drup water dropping from the eaves. Probably from the root of E. over. The s of eaves is in English regarded as a plural ending, though not so in Saxon. See Over, and cf. Eavesdrop.

ebb.etymology: AS. ebba; akin to Fries. ebba, D. eb, ebbe, Dan. & G. ebbe, Sw. ebb, cf. Goth. ibuks backward; prob. akin to E. even.

ebony.etymology: F. ébène, L. ebenus, fr. Gr. hobnim, pl. Cf. Ebon.

ebullient.etymology: L. ebulliens, -entis, p. pr. of ebullire to boil up, bubble up; e out, from + bullire to boil. See 1st Boil.

ebullition.etymology: F. ébullition, L. ebullitio, fr. ebullire. See Ebullient.

eburnation.etymology: L. eburnus of ivory, fr. ebur ivory: cf. F. éburnation. See Ivory.

ecarte.etymology: F., prop. fr. écarter to reject, discard.

eccentric.etymology: F. excentrique, formerly also spelled eccentrique, fr. LL. eccentros out of the center, eccentric, Gr. Ex-, and Center, and cf. Excentral.

roots.meaning: . A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out. as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminuos, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.

ecclesiastic.etymology: L. ecclesiasticus, Gr. Ex-, and Hale, v. t., Haul.

A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

ecdysis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. 'e`kdysis a getting out, fr. 'ekdy`ein, to put off; 'ek out + dy`ein to enter.

echelon.etymology: F., fr. échelle ladder, fr. L. scala.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

echo.etymology: L. echo, Gr. va to sound, bellow; perh. akin to E. voice: cf. F. écho.

eclat.etymology: F. éclat a fragment, splinter, explosion, brilliancy, splendor, fr. éclater to splinter, burst, explode, shine brilliantly, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. sleizan to slit, split, fr. slizan, G. schleissen; akin to E. slit.

eclectic.etymology: Gr. éclectique. See Eclogue, and cf. Elect.

eclipse.etymology: F. éclipse, L. eclipsis, fr. Gr. Ex-, and Loan.

ecliptic.etymology: Cf. F. écliptique, L. linea ecliptica, Gr. Ecliptic, a.

eclogue.etymology: L. ecloga, Gr. égloque, écloque. See Ex-, and Legend.

economic.etymology: F. économique, L. oeconomicus orderly, methodical, Gr. Economy.

economical.etymology: F. économique, L. oeconomicus orderly, methodical, Gr. Economy.

economy.etymology: F. économie, L. oeconomia household management, fr. Gr. vicus village, E. vicinity) + Vicinity, Nomad.

ecstasy.etymology: F. extase, L. ecstasis, fr. Gr. Ex-, and Stand.

eczema.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. 'e`kzema; "ek out + zei^n to boil.

edacious.etymology: L. edax, edacis, fr. edere to eat.

edda.etymology: Icel., lit. great-grandmother (i. e., of Scandinavian poetry), so called by Bishop Brynjúlf Sveinsson, who brought it again to light in 1643.

eddy.etymology: Prob. fr. Icel. i; cf. Icel. pref. i back, AS. ed-, OS. idug-, OHG. ita-; Goth. id-.

edelweiss.etymology: G., fr. edel noble + weiss white.

eden.etymology: Heb. eden delight, pleasure; also, a place of pleasure, Eden.

edentata.etymology: NL., neut. pl. from L. edentatus, p. p. of edentare to render toothless; e out + dens, dentis, tooth.

edentulous.etymology: L. edentulus; e out + dens, dentis, tooth.

edge.etymology: OE. eg, egge, AS. ecg; akin to OHG. ekka, G. ecke, Icel. & Sw. egg, Dan. eg, and to L. acies, Gr. a edge. Egg, v. t., Eager, Ear spike of corn, Acute.

edible.etymology: L. edibilis, fr. edere to eat. See Eat.

edict.etymology: L. edictum, fr. edicere, edictum, to declare, proclaim; e out + dicere to say: cf. F. édit. See Diction.

edification.etymology: L. aedificatio: cf. F. édification. See Edify.

edifice.etymology: L. aedificium, fr. aedificare: cf. F. édifice. See Edify.

edify.etymology: F. édifier, L. aedificare; aedes a building, house, orig., a fireplace (akin to Gr. idh to kindle, OHG. eit funeral pile, AS. ad, OIr. aed fire) + facere to make. See Fact, -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

edit.etymology: F. éditer, or L. editus, p. p. of edere to give out, put forth, publish; e out + dare to give. See Date a point of time.

edition.etymology: L. editio, fr. edere to publish; cf. F. édition. See Edit.

editor.etymology: L., that which produces, from edere to publish: cf. F. éditeur.

educate.etymology: L. educatus, p. p. of educare to bring up a child physically or mentally, to educate, fr. educere to Educe.

education.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French éducation , from Latin ēducātiō ( “ a breeding, bringing up, rearing ” ) , from ēducō ( “ to educate, train ” ) , from ēdūcō ( “ to lead forth, to take out; to raise up, to erect ” ) . See educate .

educe.etymology: L. educere; e out + ducere to lead. See Duke.

edulcorate.etymology: L. e oudulcoratus, p. p. of dulcorare to sweeten, fr. dulcor sweetness, fr. dulcis sweet: cf. F. édulcorer.

eel.etymology: AS. ; akin to D., G., & Dan. aal, Icel. all, Sw. ål.

efface.etymology: F. effacer; pref. es- (L. ex) + face face; prop., to destroy the face or form. See Face, and cf. Deface.

effect.etymology: L. effectus, fr. efficere, effectum, to effect; ex + facere to make: cf. F. effet, formerly also spelled effect. See Fact.

effectuate.etymology: Cf. F. effectuer. See Effect, n. & v. t.

effeminate.etymology: L. effeminatus, p. p. of effeminare to make a woman of; ex out + femina a woman. See Feminine, a.

effendi.etymology: Turk. efendi, fr. Modern Gr. Authentic.

efferent.etymology: L. efferens, -entis, p. pr. of effere to bear out; ex out + ferre to bear.

effervesce.etymology: L. effervescere; ex + fervescere to begin boiling, incho., fr. fervere to boil. See Fervent.

effervescent.etymology: L. effervescences, p. pr. of effervescere: cf. F. effervescent.

effete.etymology: L. effetus that has brought forth, exhausted; ex + fetus that has brought forth. See Fetus.

efficacious.etymology: L. eficax, -acis, fr. efficere. See Effect, n.

efficacy.etymology: L. efficacia, fr. efficax. See Efficacious.

efficient.etymology: L. efficiens, -entis, p. pr. of efficere to effect: cf. F. efficient. See Effect, n.

effigy.etymology: L. effigies, fr. effingere to form, fashion; ex + fingere to form, shape, devise. See Feign.

effloresce.etymology: L. efflorescere to bloom, blossom; ex + florescere to begin to blossom, incho., fr. florere to blossom, fr. flos a flower. See Flower.

efflorescent.etymology: F. efflorescent, L. efflorescens, -entis, blooming, p. pr. of efflorescere. See Effloresce, v. i.

effluent.etymology: L. effluens, -entis, p. pr. of effluere to flow out; ex + fluere to flow: cf. F. effluent. See Fluent.

effluvium.etymology: L., a flowing out, fr. effluere to flow out. See Effluent, a.

effort.etymology: F. effort, OF. esfort, for esfors, esforz, fr. esforcier. See Efforce.

effrontery.etymology: F. effronterie, fr. effronté shameless, fr. L. effrons, -ontis, putting forth the forehead, i. e., barefaced, shameless; ex + frons the forehead. See Front.

effulgent.etymology: L. effulgens, -entis, p. pr. of effulgere.

effuse.etymology: L. effusus, p. p. of effundere to pour out; ex + fundere to pour. See Fuse to melt.

egest.etymology: L. egestus, p. p. of egerere to carry out, to discharge; e out + gerere to carry.

egg.etymology: OE., fr. Icel. egg; akin to AS. æg (whence OE. ey), Sw. ägg, Dan. æg, G. & D. ei, and prob. to OSlav. aje, jaje, L. ovum, Gr. ugh, Gael. ubh, and perh. to L. avis bird. Cf. Oval.

eglantine.etymology: F. églantine, fr. OF. aiglent brier, hip tree, fr. (assumed) LL. acuculentus, fr. a dim. of L. acus needle; cf. F. aiguille needle. Cf. Aglet.

egoism.etymology: F. égoïsme, fr. L. -ego I. See I, and cf. Egotism.

egotism.etymology: L. ego I + ending -tism for -ism, prob. influenced by other English words in -tism fr. the Greek, where t is not part of the ending, as baptism. See Egoism.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating an act, a process, the result of an act or a process, a state; also, a characteristic (as a theory, doctrine, idiom, etc.); as, baptism, galvanism, organism, hypnotism, socialism, sensualism, Anglicism.

egotist.etymology: L. ego I + ending -tist for -ist. See Egotism, and cf. Egoist.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix denoting an agent, or doer, one who practices, a believer in; as, theorist, one who theorizes; socialist, one who holds to socialism; sensualist, one given to sensuality.

egregious.etymology: L. egregius; lit., separated or chosen from the herd, i. e., distinguished, excellent; e out + grex, gregis, herd. See Gregarious.

egress.etymology: L. egressus, fr. egredi to go out; e out + gradi to go. See Grade.

egyptian.etymology: L. Aegyptius, Gr. Aegyptus) Egypt: cf. F. égyptien. Cf. Gypsy.

eider.etymology: Of Scand. origin, cf. Icel æ; akin to Sw. eider, Dan. ederfugl.

eighteen.etymology: AS. eahtat, eahtat. See Eight, and Ten, and cf. Eighty.

eighty.etymology: AS. eahtatig, where the ending -tig is akin to English ten; cf. G. achtzig. See Eight, and Ten.

eisteddfod.etymology: W., session, fr. eistedd to sit.

either.etymology: OE. either, aither, AS. , (akin to OHG. , MHG. iegeweder); a + ge + hwæ whether. See Each, and Whether, and cf. Or, conj.

ejaculate.etymology: L. ejaculatus, p. p. of ejaculari to throw out; e out + ejaculari to throw, fr. jaculum javelin, dart, fr. jacere to throw. See Eject.

eject.etymology: L. ejectus, p. p. of ejicere; e out + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.

elaborate.etymology: L. elaboratus, p. p. of elaborare to work out; e out + laborare to labor, labor labor. See Labor.

eland.etymology: D. eland elk, of Slav. origin; cf. Pol. jelen stag, Russ. oléne, Lith. elnis; perh. akin to E. elk.

elapse.etymology: L. elapsus, p. p. of elabi to glide away; e out + labi to fall, slide. See Lapse.

elasmobranchii.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. branchia a gill.

elastic.etymology: Formed fr. Gr. alacer lively, brisk, and E. alacrity: cf. F. élastique.

roots.meaning: A suffix. See the Note under -ine.

elate.etymology: L. elatus elevated, fig., elated, proud (the figure, perh., being borrowed from a prancing horse); e out + latus (used as p. p. of ferre to bear), for tlatus, and akin to E. tolerate. See Tolerate, and cf. Extol.

elbow.etymology: AS. elboga, elnboga (akin to D. elleboga, OHG. elinbogo, G. ellbogen, ellenbogen, Icel. ; prop.; arm-bend); eln ell (orig., forearm) + boga a bending. See 1st Ell, and 4th Bow.

elder.etymology: AS. yldra, compar. of eald old. See Old.

eldest.etymology: AS. yldest, superl. of eald old. See Elder, a.

elecampane.etymology: F. énulecampane, NL. inula campana; L. inula elecampane + LL. campana a bell; cf. G. glockenwurz, i. e., "bellwort."

elect.etymology: L. electus, p. p. of eligere to elect; e out + legere to choose. See Legend, and cf. Elite, Eclectic.

election.etymology: F. élection, L. electio, fr. eligere to choose out. See Elect, a.

elector.etymology: L., fr. eligere: cf. F. électeur.

electric.etymology: L. electrum amber, a mixed metal, Gr. arc to beam, shine: cf. F. électrique. The name came from the production of electricity by the friction of amber.

electrical.etymology: L. electrum amber, a mixed metal, Gr. arc to beam, shine: cf. F. électrique. The name came from the production of electricity by the friction of amber.

electrum.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Electric, and cf. Electre, Electron.

eleemosynary.etymology: LL. eleemosynarius, fr. eleemosyna alms, Gr. Alms.

elegance.etymology: L. elegantia, fr. elegans, -antis, elegant: cf. F. élégance.

elegant.etymology: L. elegans, -antis; akin to eligere to pick out, choose, select: cf. F. élégant. See Elect.

elegiac.etymology: L. elegiacus, Gr. élégiaque. See Elegy.

elemi.etymology: Cf. F. élemi, It. elemi, Sp. elemi; of American or Oriental. origin.

elephant.etymology: OE. elefaunt, olifant, OF. olifant, F. éléphant, L. elephantus, elephas, -antis, fr. Gr. ibha, with the Semitic article al, el, prefixed, or fr. Semitic Aleph hindi Indian bull; or cf. Goth. ulbandus camel, AS. olfend.

elephantine.etymology: L. elephantinus of ivory, Gr. éléphantin.

elevator.etymology: L., one who raises up, a deliverer: cf. F. élévateur.

eleven.etymology: OE. enleven, AS. endleofan, endlufon, for nleofan; akin to LG. eleve, ölwe, ölwen, D. elf, G. elf, eilf, OHG. einlif, Icel. ellifu, Sw. elfva, Dan. elleve, Goth. ainlif, cf. Lith. vënolika; and fr. the root of E. one + (prob.) a root signifying "to be left over, remain," appearing in E. loan, or perh. in leave, v. t., life. See One, and cf. Twelve.

elf.etymology: AS. ælf, ylf; akin to MHG. alp, G. alp nightmare, incubus, Icel. elf, Sw. alf, elfva; cf. Skr. rbhu skillful, artful, rabh to grasp. Cf. Auf, Oaf.

elicit.etymology: L. elictus, p. p. of elicere to elicit; e + lacere to entice. Cf. Delight, Lace.

elide.etymology: L. elidere to strike out or off; e + laedere to hurt by striking: cf. F. élider. See Lesion.

eligible.etymology: F. éligible, fr. L. eligere. See Elect.

eliminate.etymology: L. eliminatus, p. p. of eliminare; e out + limen threshold; prob. akin to limes boundary. See Limit.

equilibrium.etymology: L. aequilibrium, fr. aequilibris in equilibrium, level; aequus equal + libra balance. See Equal, and Librate.

equine.etymology: L. equinus, fr. equus horse; akin to Gr. a, OS. ehu, AS. eh, eoh, Icel. j, OIr. ech, cf. Skr. a to reach, overtake, perh. akin to E. acute, edge, eager, a. Cf. Hippopotamus.

equinoctial.etymology: L. aequinoctials, fr. aequinoctium equinox: cf. F. équinoxial. See Equinox.

equinox.etymology: OE. equinoxium, equenoxium, L. aequinoctium; aequus equal + nox, noctis, night: cf. F. équinoxe. See Equal, and Night.

equip.etymology: F. équiper to supply, fit out, orig. said of a ship, OF. esquiper to embark; of German origin; cf. OHG. scif, G. schiff, Icel. skip, AS. scip. See Ship.

equipage.etymology: F. équipage, fr. équiper. See Equip.

roots.meaning: A prefix, meaning equally; as, equidistant; equiangular.

equisetum.etymology: L., the horsetail, fr. equus horse + seta a thick,, stiff hair, bristle.

equitable.etymology: F. équitable, from équité. See Equity.

equitation.etymology: L. equitatio, fr. equitare: cf. F. équitation.

equity.etymology: F. équité, L. aequitas, fr. aequus even, equal. See Equal.

equivalent.etymology: L. aequivalens, -entis, p. pr. of aequivalere to have equal power; aequus equal + valere to be strong, be worth: cf. F. équivalent. See Equal, and Valiant.

equivocal.etymology: L. aequivocus: aequus equal + vox, vocis, word. See Equal, and Voice, and cf. Equivoque.

equivocate.etymology: L. aequivocatus, p. p. of aequivocari to be called by the same name, fr. L. aequivocus: cf. F. équivoquer. See Equivocal, a.

era.etymology: LL. aera an era, in earlier usage, the items of an account, counters, pl. of aes, aeris, brass, money. See Ore.

eradicate.etymology: L. eradicatus, p. p. of eradicare to eradicate; e out + radix, radicis, root. See Radical.

erase.etymology: L. erasus, p. p. of eradere to erase; e out + radere to scrape, scratch, shave. See Rase.

erbium.etymology: NL. from Ytterby, in Sweden, where gadolinite is found. Cf. Terbium, Yttrium, Ytterbium.

erect.etymology: L. erectus, p. p. of erigere to erect; e out + regere to lead straight. See Right, and cf. Alert.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

ergot.etymology: F. ergot, argot, lit., a spur.

ermine.etymology: OF. ermine, F. hermine, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. harmo, G. hermelin, akin to Lith. szarm, szarmonys, weasel, cf. AS. hearma; but cf. also LL. armelinus, armellina, hermellina, and pellis Armenia, the fur of the Armenian rat, mus Armenius, the animal being found also in Armenia.

ern.etymology: AS. earn eagle; akin to D. arend, OHG. aro, G. aar, Icel., Sw., & Dan. örn, Goth. ara, and to Gr. Ornithology.

erne.etymology: AS. earn eagle; akin to D. arend, OHG. aro, G. aar, Icel., Sw., & Dan. örn, Goth. ara, and to Gr. Ornithology.

erode.etymology: L. erodere, erosum; e out + rodere to gnaw. See Rodent.

erose.etymology: L. erosus, p. p. See Erode.

err.etymology: F. errer, L. errare; akin to G. irren, OHG. irran, v. t., irr, v. i., OS. irrien, Sw. irra, Dan. irre, Goth, aírzjan to lead astray, airzise astray.

errand.etymology: OE. erende, erande, message, business, AS. ærende, ærend; akin to OS. arundi, OHG. arunti, Icel. eyrendi, örendi, erendi, Sw. ärende, Dan. ærende; perh. akin to AS. earu swift, Icel. örr, and to L. oriri to rise, E. orient.

errant.etymology: F. errant, p. pr. fr. OF. errer to travel, LL. iterare, fr. L. iter journey; confused somewhat with L. errare to err. See Eyre, and cf. Arrant, Itinerant.

erratic.etymology: L. erraticus, fr. errare to wander: cf. F. erratique. See Err.

erratum.etymology: L., fr. errare, erratum, to wander, err. See Err.

erroneous.etymology: L. erroneus, fr. errare to err. See Err.

error.etymology: OF. error, errur, F. erreur, L. error, fr. errare to err. See Err.

erse.etymology: A modification of Irish, OE. Irishe.

erst.etymology: Orig. superlative of ere; AS. . See Ere.

eruca.etymology: L., a caterpillar, also, a sort of colewort.

eruct.etymology: L. eructare; e out + ructare to belch: cf. F. éructer.

erudite.etymology: L. eruditus, p. p. of erudire to free from rudeness, to polish, instruct; e out + rudis rude: cf. F. érudit. See Rude.

eruption.etymology: L. eruptio, fr. erumpere, eruptum, to break out; e out + rumpere, to break: cf. F. éruption. See Rupture.

erysipelas.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Red, and Pell, n.

escalade.etymology: F., Sp. escalada (cf. It. scalata), fr. Sp. escalar to scale, LL. scalare, fr. L. scala ladder. See Scale, v. t.

escapade.etymology: F., fr. Sp. escapada escape, fr. escapar to escape; or F., fr. It. scappata escape, escapade, fr. scappare to escape. see Escape.

escape.etymology: OE. escapen, eschapen, OF. escaper, eschaper, F. echapper, fr. LL. ex cappa out of one's cape or cloak; hence, to slip out of one's cape and escape. See 3d Cape, and cf. Scape, v.

escarp.etymology: F. escarpe (cf. Sp. escarpa, It. scarpa), fr. escarper to cut steep, cut to a slope, prob. of German origin: cf. G. scharf sharp,, E. sharp, or perh. scrape.

eschar.etymology: L. eschara, Gr. eschare. See Scar.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

escheat.etymology: OE. eschete, escheyte, an escheat, fr. OF. escheit, escheoit, escheeite, esheoite, fr. escheoir (F. échoir) to fall to, fall to the lot of; pref. es- (L. ex) + cheoir, F. choir, to fall, fr. L. cadere. See Chance, and cf. Cheat.

eschew.etymology: OF. eschever, eschiver, eskiver, F. esquiver, fr. OHG. sciuhen, G. scheuen; akin to E. sky. See Shy, a.

eschscholtzia.etymology: NL. Named after Dr. Eschscholtz, a German botanist.

escort.etymology: F. escorte, It. scorta a guard or guide, fr. scorgere to perceive, discern, lead, fr. L. ex out, quite + corrigere to correct, set right. See Correct.

escritoire.etymology: OF. escritoire, F. écritoire, LL. scriptorium, fr. L. scriptorius belonging to writing, fr. sribere to write. See Script, and cf. Scrutoire.

escrow.etymology: OF. escroe, escroue, a roll of writings, bond. See Scroll.

escutcheon.etymology: OF. escusson, F. écusson, from OF. escu shield, F. écu. See Esquire, Scutcheon.

eskimo.etymology: Originally applied by the Algonquins to the Northern Indians, and meaning eaters of raw flesh.

espalier.etymology: F. espalier, fr. It. spalliera, fr. spalla shoulder, the same word as F. épaule. See Epaulet.

esparcet.etymology: F. esparcet, esparcette, éparcet, fr. Sp. esparceta, esparcilla.

especial.etymology: OF. especial, F. spécial, L. specialis, fr. species a particular sort, kind, or quality. See Species, and cf. Special.

espial.etymology: OE. & Norm. F. espiaille. See Espy.

espionage.etymology: F. espionnage, fr. espionner to spy, fr. espion spy, OF. espie. See Espy.

esplanade.etymology: F. esplanade, Sp. esplanada, explanada, cf. It. spianata; fr. Sp. explanar to level, L. explanare to flatten or spread out. See Explain.

espousal.etymology: OF. espousailles, pl., F. épousailles, L. sponsalia, fr. sponsalis belonging to betrothal or espousal. See Espouse, and cf. Sponsal, Spousal.

espouse.etymology: OF. espouser, esposer, F. épouser, L. sponsare to betroth, espouse, fr. sponsus betrothed, p. p. of spondere to promise solemnly or sacredly. Cf. Spouse.

espy.etymology: OF. espier, F. épier, from OHG. speh to watch, spy, G. spähen; akin to L. specere to look, species sight, shape, appearance, kind. See Spice, Spy, and cf. Espionage.

esquire.etymology: OF. escuyer, escuier, properly, a shield-bearer, F. écuyer shield-bearer, armor-bearer, squire of a knight, esquire, equerry, rider, horseman, LL. scutarius shield-bearer, fr. L. scutum shield, akin to Gr. to cover; prob. akin to E. hide to cover. See Hide to cover, and cf. Equerry, Escutcheon.

essay.etymology: F. essai, fr. L. exagium a weighing, weight, balance; ex out + agere to drive, do; cf. examen, exagmen, a means of weighing, a weighing, the tongue of a balance, exigere to drive out, examine, weigh, Gr. 'exa`gion a weight, 'exagia`zein to examine, 'exa`gein to drive out, export. See Agent, and cf. Exact, Examine, Assay.

essence.etymology: F. essence, L. essentia, formed as if fr. a p. pr. of esse to be. See Is, and cf. Entity.

essene.etymology: Gr. asaya to heal, cf. Heb. asa.

essonite.etymology: Named from Gr. e. g., hyacinth.

establish.etymology: OE. establissen, OF. establir, F. établir, fr. L. stabilire, fr. stabilis firm, steady, stable. See Stable, a., - ish, and cf. Stablish.

estate.etymology: OF. estat, F. état, L. status, fr. stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. State.

esteem.etymology: F. estimer, L. aestimare, aestumare, to value, estimate; perh. akin to Skr. ish to seek, strive, and E. ask. Cf. Aim, Estimate.

ester.etymology: A word invented by L. Gmelin, a German chemist.

estimable.etymology: F. estimable, or L. aestimabilis. See Esteem.

estimate.etymology: L. aestimatus, p. p. of aestimare. See Esteem, v. t.

estimation.etymology: L. aestimatio, fr. aestimare: cf. F. estimation. See Esteem, v. t.

estrange.etymology: OF. estrangier to remove, F. étranger, L. extraneare to treat as a stranger, from extraneus strange. See Strange.

estuary.etymology: L. aestuarium, from aestuare to surge. See Estuate.

esurient.etymology: L. esuriens, p. pr. of ensurire, fr. edere to eat.

etagere.etymology: F., fr. étager to arrange on shelves, fr. étage story, floor. See Stage.

etch.etymology: D. etsen, G. ätzen to feed, corrode, etch. MHG. etzen, causative of ezzen to eat, G. essen Eat.

eternal.etymology: F. éternel, L. aeternalis, fr. aeternus. See Etern.

eternity.etymology: F. éternité, L. aeternitas, fr. aeternus. See Etern.

ether.etymology: L. aether, Gr. idh, indh, and prob. to E. idle: cf. F. éther.

ethic.etymology: L. ethicus, Gr. sidus, G. sitte, Skr. svadh, prob. orig., one's own doing; sva self + dh to set: cf. F. éthique. See So, Do.

ethical.etymology: L. ethicus, Gr. sidus, G. sitte, Skr. svadh, prob. orig., one's own doing; sva self + dh to set: cf. F. éthique. See So, Do.

ethos.etymology: L., fr. Gr. character. See Ethic.

etiquette.etymology: F. prop., a little piece of paper, or a mark or title, affixed to a bag or bundle, expressing its contents, a label, ticket, OF.estiquete, of German origin; cf. LG. stikke peg, pin, tack, stikken to stick, G. stecken. See Stick, and cf. Ticket.

etymological.etymology: L. etymologicus, Gr. étimilogique. See Etymology.

etymology.etymology: L.etymologia, Gr. étymologie. See Etymon, and -logy.

etymon.etymology: L., fr. Gr. sotya, E. sooth. See Sooth.

eucharist.etymology: L. euchaistia, Gr. yearn: cf. F. euchaistie.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

eugenia.etymology: NL. Named in honor of Prince Eugene of Savoy.

eupatorium.etymology: NL., fr. Eupator, king of Pontus, said to have used it as a medicine.

euphorbia.etymology: NL., fr. L. euphorbea. See Euphorrium.

euphorbium.etymology: NL., fr. L. euphorbeum, from Gr. Euphorbus, a Greek physician.

euphuism.etymology: Gr. Euphues, or the Anatomy of Wit," and "Euphues and his England."

euryale.etymology: NL., fr. Euryale, one of the Gorgons.

eutectic.etymology: Gr. e'y`thktos easily melted; e'y^ well + th`kein to melt.

evacuant.etymology: L.evacuans, -antis, p. pr. of evacuare: cf. F. évacuant.

evacuate.etymology: l. evacuatus, p. p. of evacuare to empty, nullify; e out + vacuus empty, vacare to be empty. See Vacate.

evade.etymology: L. evadere, evasum, e out + vadere to go, walk: cf. F. s'évader. See Wade.

evanesce.etymology: L. evanescere; e out + vanescere to vanish, fr. vanus empty, vain. See Vain, and cf. Evanish.

evanescent.etymology: L. evanescens, -entis, p. pr. of evanescere.

evangel.etymology: F. évangile, L. evangelium, Gr. Eu-, and cf. Evangely.

evaporate.etymology: L. evaporatus, p. p. of evaporare; e out + vapor steam or vapor. See Vapor.

evaporometer.etymology: L. evaporare to evaporate + -meter: cf. F. évapormètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

evasion.etymology: L. evasio: cf. F. évasion. See Evade.

even.etymology: OE. eve, even, efen, æfen. AS. æfen; akin to OS. aband, OFries, avend, D. avond, OHG. aband, Icel. aptan, Sw. afton, Dan. aften; of unknown origin. Cf. Eve, Evening.

evening.etymology: AS. æfnung. See even, n., and cf. Eve.

event.etymology: L. eventus, fr. evenire to happen, come out; e out + venire to come. See Come.

ever.etymology: OE. ever, æfre, AS. æfre; perh. akin to AS. a always. Cf. Aye, Age,Evry, Never.

evict.etymology: L. evictus, p. p. of evincere to overcome completely, evict. See Evince.

evidence.etymology: F. évidence, L. Evidentia. See Evident.

evil.etymology: OE. evel, evil, ifel, uvel, AS. yfel; akin to OFries, evel, D. euvel, OS. & OHG. ubil, G. übel, Goth. ubils, and perh. to E. over.

evince.etymology: L. evincere vanquish completely, prevail, succeed in proving; e out + vincere to vanquish. See Victor, and cf. Evict.

eviscerate.etymology: L. evisceratus, p. p. of eviscerare to eviscerate; e out + viscera the bowels. See Viscera.

evoke.etymology: L. evocare; e out + vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F évoquer. See Voice, and cf. Evocate.

evolution.etymology: L. evolutio an unrolling: cf. F. évolution evolution. See Evolve.

evolve.etymology: L. evolvere, evolutum; e out + volvere to roll. See Voluble.

ewe.etymology: AS. eówu; akin to D. ooi, OHG. awi, ouwi, Icel. ær, Goth. awe\'edi a flock of sheep, awistr a sheepfold, Lith. avis a sheep, L. ovis, Gr. avi. *231.

ewer.etymology: OF. ewer, euwier, prop. a water carrier, F. évier a washing place, sink, aiguière ewer, L. aquarius, adj., water carrying, n., a water carrier, fr. aqua water; akin to Goth. ahwa water, river, OHG, aha, G. au, aue, meadow. *219. Cf. Aquarium, Aquatic, Island.

exacerbate.etymology: L. exacerbatus, p. p. of exacerbare; ex out (intens.) + acerbare. See Acerbate.

exact.etymology: L. exactus precise, accurate, p. p. of exigere to drive out, to demand, enforce, finish, determine, measure; ex out + agere to drive; cf. F. exact. See Agent, Act.

exaggerate.etymology: Borrowed from Latin exaggerātus , perfect passive participle of exaggerō ( “ to heap up, increase, enlarge, magnify, amplify, exaggerate ” ) (see -ate ( verb-forming suffix ) and -ate ( adjective-forming suffix ) ), from ex- ( “ out, up ” ) + aggerō, aggerāre ( “ to heap up ” ) , from agger ( “ a pile, heap, mound, dike, mole, pier, etc. ” ) , from aggerō, aggerere ( “ to bear, carry to (some place), bring together ” ) , from ad- ( “ to, toward ” ) +‎ gerō ( “ to carry ” ) .

exalt.etymology: L. exaltare; ex out (intens.) + altare to make high, altus high: cf.F. exalter. See Altitude.

examen.etymology: L., the tongue of a balance, examination; for exagmen, fr. exigere to weigh accurately, to treat: cf. F. examen. See Exact, a.

examine.etymology: L. examinare, examinatum, fr. examen, examinis: cf. F. examiner. See Examen.

example.etymology: A later form for ensample, fr. L. exemplum, orig., what is taken out of a larger quantity, as a sample, from eximere to take out. See Exempt, and cf. Ensample, Sample.

exanimate.etymology: L. exanimatus, p. p. of exanimare to deprive of life or spirit; ex out + anima air, breath, life, spirit.

exarchate.etymology: LL. exarchatus, fr. L. exarchus: cf. F. exarchat.

exasperate.etymology: L. exasperatus, p. p. of exsasperare to roughen, exasperate; ex out (intens.) + asperare to make rough, asper rough. See Asperity.

excavate.etymology: L. excavatus, p. p. of excavare to excavate; ex out + cavare to make hollow, cavus hollow. See Cave.

exceed.etymology: L. excedere, excessum, to go away or beyond; ex out + cedere to go, to pass: cf. F. excéder. See Cede.

excel.etymology: L. excellere, excelsum; ex out + a root found in culmen height, top; cf. F. exceller. See Culminate, Column.

excellent.etymology: F. excellent, L. excellens, -entis, p. pr. of excellere. See Excel.

excelsior.etymology: L., compar. of excelsus elevated, lofty, p. p. of excellere. See Excel, v. t.

except.etymology: L. exceptus, p. p. of excipere to take or draw out, to except; ex out + capere to take: cf. F. excepter. See Capable.

excerpt.etymology: From L. excerptus, p. p. See Excerp.

excess.etymology: OE. exces, excess, ecstasy, L. excessus a going out, loss of self-possession, fr. excedere, excessum, to go out, go beyond: cf. F. excès. See Exceed.

exchange.etymology: OE. eschange, eschaunge, OF. eschange, fr. eschangier, F. échanger, to exchange; pref. ex- out + F. changer. See Change, and cf. Excamb.

roots.meaning: . A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out. as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminuos, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.

exchequer.etymology: OE. escheker, OF. eichekier, fr. LL. scaccarium. See Checker, Chess, Check.

excise.etymology: Apparently fr. L. excisum cut off, fr. excidere to cut out or off; ex out, off + caedere to cut; or, as the word was formerly written accise, fr. F. accise, LL. accisia, as if fr. L. accidere, accisum, to cut into; ad + caedere to cut; but prob. transformed fr. OF. assise, LL. assisa, assisia, assize. See Assize, Concise.

excision.etymology: L. excisio: cf. F. excision. See Excide.

excitable.etymology: L. excitabilis inciting: cf. F. excitable.

excitant.etymology: L. excitans, -antis, p. pr. of excitare: cf. F. excitant.

excite.etymology: L. excitare; ex out + citare to move rapidly, to rouse: cf. OF. esciter, exciter, F. exciter. See Cite.

exclaim.etymology: L. exclamare, exclamatum; ex + clamare to cry out; cf. OF. exclamer. See Clam.

exclude.etymology: L. excludere, exclusum; ex out + claudere to shut. See Close.

exclusion.etymology: L. exclusio: cf. F. exclusion. See Exclude.

excogitate.etymology: L. excogitatus, p. p. of excogitare to excogitate; ex out + cogitare to think. See Cogitate.

excommunicate.etymology: L. excommunicatus, p. p. of communicare to excommunicate; ex out + communicare. See Communicate.

excoriate.etymology: L. excoriare; ex out + corium hide. cf. Scourge; see Cuirass.

excrement.etymology: L. excrementum, fr. excernere, excretum, to skin out, discharge: cf. F. excrément. See Excrete.

excrescence.etymology: F. excrescence, excroissanse, L. excrescentia excrescences, neut. pl. of p. pr. of excrescere. See Excrescent.

excrescent.etymology: L. excresens, -entis, p. pr. of excrescere to grow out ; ex out + crescere to grow. See Crescent.

excrete.etymology: L. excretus, p. p. of excernere to sift out, discharge; ex out + cernere to sift, separate. See Crisis.

excruciate.etymology: L. excruciatus, p. p. of excruciare to excruciate; ex out + cruciare to put to death on a cross, to torment. See Cruciate, Cross.

exculpate.etymology: L. ex out + culpatus, p. p. of culpare to find fault with, to blame, culpa fault. See Culpable.

excursion.etymology: L. excursio: cf. F. excursion. See Excurrent.

excursus.etymology: L., fr. excurrere, excursum. See Excurrent.

excusable.etymology: L. excusabilis: cf. F. excusable. See Excuse.

excuse.etymology: OE. escusen, cusen, OF. escuser, excuser, F. excuser, fr. L. excusare; ex out + causa cause, causari to plead. See Cause.

execrable.etymology: L. execrabilis, exsecrabilis: cf. F. exécrable. See Execrate.

execrate.etymology: L. execratus, exsecratus, p. p. of execrare, exsecrare, to execrate; ex out + sacer holy, sacred. See Sacred.

execration.etymology: L. execratio, exsecratio: cf. F. exécration.

execute.etymology: F. exécuter, L. executus, exsecutus, p. p. of exequi to follow to the end, pursue; ex out + sequi to follow. See Second, Sue to follow up, and cf. Exequy.

executor.etymology: L. executor, exsecutor: cf. F. exécuteur. Cf. Executer.

exemplar.etymology: L. exemplar, exemplum: cf. F. exemplaire. See Example, and cf. Examper, Sampler.

exemplary.etymology: L. exemplaris, fr. exemplar: cf. F. exemplaire. See Exemplar.

exemplify.etymology: L. exemplum example + -fy: cf. LL. exemplificare to copy, serve as an example.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

exempt.etymology: F. exempt, L. exemptus, p. p. of eximere to take out, remove, free; ex out + emere to buy, take. Cf. Exon, Redeem.

exemption.etymology: L. exenptio a removing: cf. F. exemption exemption.

exercise.etymology: F. exercice, L. exercitium, from exercere, exercitum, to drive on, keep, busy, prob. orig., to thrust or drive out of the inclosure; ex out + arcere to shut up, inclose. See Ark.

exert.etymology: L. exertus, exsertus, p.p. of exerere, exserere, to thrust out; ex out + serere to join or bind together. See Series, and cf. Exsert.

exfoliate.etymology: L. exfoliare to strip of leaves; ex out, from + folium leaf.

exhalation.etymology: L. exhalatio: cf. F. exhalaison, exhalation.

exhale.etymology: L. exhalare; ex out + halare to breathe; cf.F. exhaler. Cf. Inhale.

exhaust.etymology: L. exhaustus, p.p. of exhaurire; ex out + haurire, haustum, to draw, esp. water; perhaps akin to Icel. asua to sprinkle, pump.

exhibit.etymology: L. exhibitus, p. p. of exhibere to hold forth, to tender, exhibit; ex out + habere to have or hold. See Habit.

exhibition.etymology: L. exhibitio a delivering: cf. F. exhibition.

exhilarate.etymology: L. exhilaratus, p.p. of exhilarare to gladden; ex out + hilarare to make merry, hilaris merry, cheerful. See Hilarious.

exhort.etymology: L. exhortari; ex out + hortari to incite, encourage; cf. F. exhorter. See Hortative.

exhume.etymology: LL. exhumare; L. ex out + humus ground, soil: cf. F. exhumer. See Humble.

exigent.etymology: L. exigens, -entis, p. pr. of exigere to drive out or forth, require, exact. See Exact.

exiguity.etymology: L. exiguitas, fr. exiguus small: cf. F. exiguité.

exile.etymology: OE. exil, fr. L. exilium, exsilium, fr. exsuil one who quits, or is banished from, his native soil; ex out + solum ground, land, soil, or perh. fr.the root of salire to leap, spring; cf. F. exil. Cf. Sole of the foot, Saltation.

exist.etymology: L. existere, exsistere, to step out or forth, emerge, appear, exist; ex out + sistere to cause to stand, to set, put, place, stand still, fr. stare to stand: cf. F. exister. See Stand.

existent.etymology: L. existens, -entis, p. pr. of existere. See Exist.

exit.etymology: L., 3d pers. sing. pres. of exire to go out. See Exeunt, Issue.

exmoor.etymology: From Exmoor, a district in Somersetshire and Devonshire.

exode.etymology: L. exodium, Gr. exode. See Exodus.

exodus.etymology: L., the book of Exodus, Gr. Skr. a-sad to approach.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying out of, outside; as in exocarp, exogen, exoskeleton.

exon.etymology: NL., from E. Exe (Celt. uisge water) the name of a river.

exonerate.etymology: L. exoneratus, p. p. of exonerare to free from a burden; ex out, from onerare to load, onus load. See Onerous.

exorbitant.etymology: L. exorbitans, -antis, p. pr. of exorbitare to go out of the track; ex out + orbita track: cf. F. exorbitant. See Orbit.

exorcism.etymology: L. exorcismus, Gr. ; cf. F. exorcisme.

exordium.etymology: L. fr. exordiri to begin a web, lay a warp, begin; ex out + ordiri to begin a web, begin; akin to E. order. See Order.

exoteric.etymology: L. exotericus, Gr. exotérique. See Ex-

roots.meaning: . A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out. as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminuos, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.

exotic.etymology: L. exoticus, Gr. exotique. See Exoteric.

expand.etymology: L. expandere, expansum; ex out + pandere to spread out, to throw open; perh. akin to E. patent. Cf. Spawn.

expanse.etymology: From L. expansus, p. p. of expandere. See Expand.

expatiate.etymology: L. expatiatus, exspatiatus, p. p. of expatiari, exspatiari, to expatiate; ex out + spatiari to walk about spread out, fr. spatium space. See Space.

expatriate.etymology: LL. expatriatus, p. p. of expatriare; L. ex out + patria fatherland, native land, fr. pater father. See Patriot.

expect.etymology: L. expectatum, to look out for, await, expect; ex + out spectare to look at. See Spectacle.

expectant.etymology: L.expectans, exspectans, p.pr. of expectare, exspectare: cf. F. expectant.

expectation.etymology: L. expectio. exspectio: cf. F. expectation.

expectorant.etymology: L. expectorans, p. pr. of expectorare to drive from the breast: cf. F. expectorant.

expectorate.etymology: L. expecrorare to drive from the breast; ex out + pectus, pectiris, breast. See Pectoral.

expedient.etymology: L. expediens, -entis, p. pr. of expedire to be expedient, release, extricate: cf. F. expédient. See Expedite.

expedite.etymology: L. expeditus, p. p. of expedire to free one caught by the foot, to extricate, set free, bring forward, make ready; ex out + pes, prdis, t. See Foot.

expel.etymology: L. expellere, expulsum; ex out + pellere to drive: cf.F. expeller. See Pulse a beat.

expend.etymology: L. expendere, expensum, to weigh out, pay out, lay out, lay out; ex out + pendere to weigh. See Poise, and cf. Spend.

expense.etymology: L. expensa (sc. pecunia), or expensum, fr. expensus, p. p. of expendere. See Expend.

experience.etymology: From Middle English experience , from Old French , from Latin experientia ( “ a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience ” ) , from experiens , present participle of experiri ( “ to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo ” ) , from ex ( “ out ” ) + peritus ( “ experienced, expert ” ) , past participle of *periri ( “ to go through ” ) ; see expert and peril . Displaced native Old English āfandung ( “ experience ” ) and āfandian ( “ to experience ” ) .

experiment.etymology: L. experimentum, fr. experiri to try: cf. OF. esperiment, experiment. See Experience.

expert.etymology: F. expert, L. expertus, p. p. of experiri to try. See Experience.

expiate.etymology: L. expiatus, p.p. of expiare to expiate; ex out + piare to seek to appease, to purify with sacred rites, fr. pius pious. See Pious.

expiration.etymology: L. expiratio,exspiratio: cf. F. expiration. See Expire.

expire.etymology: L. expirare, exspirare, expiratum, exspiratum; ex out + spirare to breathe: cf. F. expirer. See Spirit.

explain.etymology: L. explandare to flatten, spread out, explain; ex out+plandare to make level or plain, planus plain: cf. OF. esplaner, explaner. See Plain,a., and cf. Esplanade.

expletive.etymology: L. expletivus, from expletus, p.p. of explere to fill up; ex out+plere to fill, akin to plenus full: cf. F. explétif. See Full.

explicit.etymology: LL., an abbreviation of explicitus (est liber) the book (which anciently was a roll of parchment) is unfolded (and, of course, "finished"). See Explicit, a.

explode.etymology: L. explodere, explosum, to drive out, drive out a player by clapping; ex out+plaudere, plodere, to clap, strike, applaud: cf. OF. exploder. See Plausible.

exploit.etymology: OE. esploit success, OF. esploit, espleit,revenue, product, vigor, force, exploit, F. exploit exploit, fr. L. explicitum, prop. p.p. neut. of explicare to unfold, display, exhibit; ex+plicare to fold. See Ply, and cf. Explicit, Explicate.

explore.etymology: L. explorare to explore; ex out+plorare to cry out aloud,prob. orig., to cause to flow; perh. akin to E. flow: cf. F. explorer.

explosion.etymology: L. explosio a driving off by clapping: cf. F. explosion explosion. See Explode.

exponent.etymology: L. exponens, -entis, p. pr. of exponere to put out, set forth, expose. See Expound.

export.etymology: L. exportare, exportatum; ex out+portare to carry : cf. F. exporter. See Port demeanor.

expose.etymology: F. exposer; pref. ex- (L. ex out)+poser to place. See Pose, v. t.

exposition.etymology: L. expositio, fr. exponere, expositum: cf. F. exposition. See Expound.

expostulate.etymology: L. expostulatus, p.p. of expostulare to demand vehemently; ex out + postulare to ask, require. See Postulate.

expound.etymology: OE. exponen, expounen, expounden, fr. L. exponere to set out, expose, expound; ex out + ponere to put: cf. OE. expondre, expondre. See Position.

express.etymology: F. exprès, L. expressus, p.p. of exprimere to express; ex. out + premere To press. See Press.

expropriate.etymology: L. ex out, from + proprius one's own: cf. F. exproprier.

expulsion.etymology: L. expulsio, fr. expellere: cf. F. expulsion. See Expel.

expunction.etymology: L. expunctio execution, performance, from expungere. See Expunge.

expunge.etymology: L. expungere, expunctum, prick out, expunge, settle an account, execute; ex out + pungere to prick, puncture. See Pungent.

expurgate.etymology: L. expurgatus, p.p. of expurgare to purge, purify; ex out, from + purgare to cleanse, purify, purge. See Purge, and cf. Spurge.

expurgation.etymology: L. expurgatio justification, excuse: cf. F. expurgation.

exquisite.etymology: L. exquisitus, p.p. of exquirere to search out; ex out + quarere to seek, search. See Quest.

exsert.etymology: L. exsertus, p.p. of exserere to stretch out or forth. See Exert.

exsiccate.etymology: L. exsiccatus, p.p. of exsiccare to dry up; ex out + siccare to make dry, siccus dry.

extant.etymology: L. extans, -antis, or exstans, -antis, p.pr. of extare, exstare, to stand out or forth; ex out + stare to stand: cf. F. extant. See Stand.

extempore.etymology: L. ex out + tempus, temporis, time. See Temporal.

extend.etymology: L. extendere, extentum, extensum; ex out + tendere to stretch. See Trend.

extension.etymology: L. extensio: cf. F. extension. See Extend, v. t.

extensive.etymology: L. extensivus: cf. F. extensif. See Extend.

extensor.etymology: L., one who stretches. See Extend.

extent.etymology: L. extentus, p. p. of extendere. See Extend.

extenuate.etymology: L. extenuatus, p. p. of extenuare to make thin, loosen, weaken; ex out + tenuare to make thin, tenuis thin. See Tenuity.

exterior.etymology: L. exterior, compar. of exter or exterus on the outside, outward, foreign, strange, a compar. fr. ex: cf. F. extérieur. See Ex, and cf. Extreme, Interior.

exterminate.etymology: L. exterminatus, p. p. of exterminare to abolish, destroy, drive out or away; ex out + terminus boundary, limit. See Term.

external.etymology: L. externus, fr. exter, exterus, on the outside, outward. See Exterior.

extinct.etymology: L. extinctus, exstinctus, p. p. of extinguere, exstinguere. See Extinguish.

extinction.etymology: L. extinctio, exstinction: cf. F. extinction.

extinguish.etymology: L. extinguere, exstinguere; ex out + stinguere to quench. See Distinguish, Finish.

extirpate.etymology: L. extirpatus, exstirpatus, p. p. of extirpare, exstirpare; ex out + strips stock, stem, root.

extirpation.etymology: L. extirpatio, exstirpatio: cf. F. extirpation.

extol.etymology: L. extollere; ex out + tollere to lift, take up, or raise: cf. OF. extoller. See Tollerate, and cf. Flate.

extort.etymology: L. extortus, p. p. of extorquere to twist or wrench out, to extort; ex out + torquere to turn about, twist. See Torsion.

extract.etymology: L. extractus, p. p. of extrahere to extract; ex out + trahere to draw. See Trace, and cf. Estreat.

extradition.etymology: L. ex out + traditio a delivering up: cf. F. extradition. See Tradition.

extrados.etymology: F.; pref. extra outside + dos (L. dorsum) the back.

extraneous.etymology: L. extraneus, from extra. See Extra, Strange.

extraordinary.etymology: L. extraordinarius; extra on the outside + ordinarius: cf. F. extraordinaire. See Ordinary.

extravagance.etymology: Cf. F. extravagance. See Extravagant, and cf. Extravaganza.

extravagant.etymology: F. extravagant, fr. L. extra on the outside + vagance, , p. pr. of vagari to wander, from vagus wandering, vague. See Vague.

extravaganza.etymology: Extravagance with an Italian ending: cf. It. stravaganza.

extravasate.etymology: Pref. extra + L. vas vessel: cf. F. extravaser. See Vase.

extraversion.etymology: Pref. extra + L. vertere, versum, to turn: cf. F. extraversion.

extreme.etymology: L. extremus, superl. of exter, extrus, on the outside, outward: cf. F. extrême. See Exterior.

extricate.etymology: L. extricatus, p. p. of extricare to extricate; ex out + tricae trifles, impediments, perplexities. Cf. Intricate.

extrinsic.etymology: L. extrinsecus; exter on the outside + secus otherwise, beside; akin to E. second: cf. F. extrinsèque. See Exterior, Second.

extrude.etymology: L. extrudere, extrusum; ex out + trudere to thrust, akin to E. threat. See Threat.

exuberant.etymology: L. exuberans, exuberantis, p. pr. of exuberare to be abundant; ex + uberare to be fruitful, fr. uber fruitful, fertile, uber udder: cf. F. exubérant. See Udder.

exuberate.etymology: L. exuberatus, p. p. of exuberare. See Exuberant, n.

exude.etymology: L. exudare, exsudare, exudatum, exsudatum, to sweat out; ex out + sudare to sweat: cf. F. exuder, exsuder. See Sweat.

exult.etymology: L. exultare, exsultare, exultatum, exsultatum, to leap vigorously, to exult, intens. fr. exsilire to spring out or up; ex out + salire to spring, leap: cf. F. exulter. See Salient.

exultant.etymology: L. exsultans, exsultantis, p. pr. of exsultare. See Exult.

exuviae.etymology: L., fr. exuere to draw out or off, to pull off.

eyas.etymology: F.niais fresh from the nest, a derivative fr. L. nidus nest. E. an eyas for a nias. See Nest, and cf. Nias, Jashawk.

eye.etymology: Prob. fr. nye, an eye being for a nye. See Nye.

eyelet.etymology: F., dim. of oculus. See Eye, and cf. Oillet.

eyre.etymology: OF. erre journey, march, way, fr. L. iter, itineris, a going, way, fr. the root of ire to go. Cf. Errant, Itinerant, Issue.
